# Continual-ARC demo discipline

## Workflow
1. Parse each region, background, object colors, divider orientation, and dimensions from the current instance. Treat task IDs and remembered task-specific rules as hypotheses only; recurring tasks may vary in geometry and palette.
2. Compare every demo input-output pair cell-by-cell. Identify equality/inequality mappings, output palette, row/column orientation, and unchanged cases. Explain all observations with one consistent rule before submitting.
3. Choose demos by information value. If candidate rules remain ambiguous and a wrong submission costs more than a demo, request a demo that distinguishes them. Do not spend attempts on speculative palette or orientation variants.
4. After an incorrect submission, explicitly discard the hypothesis it tested. Reassess all of the test and demos; do not repeat uniform grids, near-identical masks, or cosmetic color changes. Before a later submission, verify each output coordinate, dimensions, and palette against the rule and examples.
5. Maintain the interface contract on every turn: output exactly one valid JSON action object on the final line, with no explanation or extra text. Valid actions are `submit`, `request_demos`, or `finish` only when the instance is over. Do not use `finish` prematurely.

## task-489a9ff2 fresh instance (16x29) unresolved — four demos, eight rejected submissions

Test consists of multiple isolated outlined rectangles with blank interiors and a few singleton-marker interiors. Four demos in this exact instance established a strong local transformation: preserve frame borders/exterior; recolor blank strict interiors to 2, while a single-cell marked interior becomes 7. Demo 1: bg8, 4-frame interior 2x2 ->2; 0-frame 4x4->2; 0-frame 6x6->2; 9-frame singleton marker ->7. Demo 2: 9-frame 2x2->2, 8-frame 4x5->7, 1-frame 3x3->7. Demo 3: 9-frame 2x2->2 and 8-frame 2x2->2. Demo 4: 3-frame 4x4->2; 6-frame 2x2->2; 8-frame singleton->7. Thus both interior contents and/or outer dimensions/context may matter; blank interiors commonly map 2, singleton maps 7, but demo 2's large blank 4x5 interior mapped 7 and blocks a simple blank->2 rule.

Test features (0-indexed): frame color1 rows0-2 cols19-21, singleton center (1,20); frame color1 rows4-11 cols10-17 with strict interior rows5-10 cols11-16 (6x6 blank); frame color4 rows4-8 cols22-26, interior rows5-7 cols23-25 (3x3 blank); frame color6 rows10-12 cols0-2, singleton center (11,1); frame color9 rows11-13 cols5-7, singleton center (12,6); frame color3 rows10-13 cols22-25, interior rows11-12 cols23-24 (2x2 blank). Eight rejected outputs all preserved shapes and variously filled subsets with 2 and/or 7; no rule obtained. Rejected variants largely assigned broad 2 to large blank spaces and 7 to singleton markers, changing which objects were filled. Do not repeat these assumptions/guesses. Main unresolved anomaly: demo2 blank 4x5 ->7 while other blank regions including 4x4, 2x2, 6x6 ->2. Could be relation to frame color/shape/context, not solely area or interior content. Need a demo varying one factor, especially blank 4x5 vs other sizes or same outline color with different dimensions, to resolve. Preserve uncertainty; don't make blind palette variants.

### Solved 11x18 instance: recolor all closed frame interiors by area parity
Preserve frame borders and exterior/background. Fill every strict rectangular interior: odd number of interior cells -> color 7; even number -> color 2. Demos confirmed 1x1, 3x3, 5x5 interiors -> 7; 2x2, 4x4, 6x6 -> 2. The proven invariant is interior-cell-count parity; observed interiors happened to be squares.

Solved test had THREE frames, including an easy-to-miss large color-3 frame: color-5 frame rows1-3, cols0-2 had 1x1 interior at (2,1) ->7; color-8 frame rows6-9, cols1-4 had 2x2 interior rows7-8, cols2-3 ->2; color-3 frame rows0-7, cols6-13 had 6x6 interior rows1-6, cols7-12 ->2. All other cells/borders unchanged. Accepted output was submitted in this session.

Failure lesson: the first three rejected submissions omitted the large frame's 6x6 interior (and varied fills on the two small interiors). The successful submission recolored all three. Always scan the entire grid for every enclosed frame, including large ones; do not stop after the obvious small objects. Historical task notes can conflict across recurrences; the above is confirmed for this instance by the demos and accepted answer.
A current 28x23 instance contains outlined rectangles with interiors: color-0 outline at rows 8-11, cols 7-10 (2x2 interior); color-3 outline rows 9-11 cols 17-19 (1x1 interior); color-4 outline rows 14-20 cols 15-21 (5x5 interior); color-5 outlines rows 17-20 cols 0-3 (2x2), rows 16-19 cols 5-8 (2x2), rows 18-20 cols 11-13 (1x1); color-8 outline rows 22-24 cols 12-14 (1x1). Earlier memory says dimension-based recoloring, but submissions applying 1x1->7, 2x2->2, 5x5->2 or background were rejected repeatedly. Six demos in that run established only varying interior fills, not a stable size rule: demo1 2x2 interior -> 7, 6x6 ->2; demo2 2x2 ->7, 2x2 ->7, 1x1->7, 3x3->2, 3x3->7; demo3 4x4->2, 3x3->7, 1x1->7; demo4 3x3->7, 6x6->2, 2x2->2; demo5 3x3->7 and 1x1->7; demo6 6x6->2 and 4x4->2. The key unresolved issue is a contextual mapping beyond just geometric size. Eight submitted grids failed; all retained original-size geometry and variously inserted 2/7 in interiors. Do not repeat a size-only palette rule. Request demos and compare rectangle outline color, interior size, location/context, and neighboring shapes; preserve outlines/background.

## task-38f52b9d: separator lines and special column (demo-confirmed)

Rule: Recolor every full uniform row to 2. Full uniform rows include both separator rows (background color) and any uniform rows of the other color; do not recolor uniform columns wholesale. In addition, recolor the distinguished column to 2: demos establish this as the column whose input color matches the separator color / recurring separator-line color, while preserving all its non-uniform line companions (only the cells in that column change). In Demo 1 (26x12), every row that is all 5 became all 2; rows with pattern 4/5 remained unchanged except column 4 (0-indexed), where every cell became 2. In Demo 2 (12x25), every all-6 row became all 2; columns 0,4,8,14,20 were all 6 in the input and became 2, reflecting the recurring vertical separators (not arbitrary uniform columns—some columns with other values remain untouched). Demo 3 (24x24) confirms full uniform rows all 8 -> 2 and two internal vertical lines c10 and c16 of 8 -> 2, while other 8 markers remain unchanged. Thus detect the grid's structural vertical separator column(s) from repeated aligned full-height / near-full-height columns of the separator color, rather than changing all columns of any uniform color. In the solved test (20x10), rows 3,4,5,8,10 were uniform 6 and became 2; column 4 was the internal separator, all 6 there became 2; every other cell stayed exactly as input. A further accepted recurrence (9x18, palette 3/9) has uniform rows 3 and 5 (0-based), and full-height uniform columns 2 (all 3) and 17 (all 3). The correct transformation recolors those full uniform rows and columns to 2, preserving every other cell. This recurrence confirms full uniform columns can be part of the separator structure; in the test, columns 2 and 17 were both entirely 3. Rejected hypothesis: globally recoloring every uniform column is incorrect in examples with structural separator selection; identify columns supported by current demo patterns. Validate output dimensions and preserve all remaining pixels.

Earlier resolved recurrence memory had an overgeneralized “recolor all uniform rows and columns” claim; treat it as superseded. The demonstrations show aligned separator structure, not a simple uniform-line rule for columns.


## Paired-band comparison pattern
When a solid full-width row or full-height column separates two aligned bands, exclude the divider and compare corresponding cells. A common learned mapping is equality => 3 and inequality => the first band's background; determine that background from the full band rather than assuming its most visually prominent color. Horizontal divider: compare upper/lower bands; vertical divider: compare left/right. Confirm the exact palette and mapping from current demos rather than importing this pattern blindly.

## Pitfalls
- A known task ID or memory is not a substitute for current demo evidence.
- Do not confuse equal-cell locations with marker overlaps alone: background-background matches may also map to the equality color.
- A rejection is evidence; change the rule/model, not merely the output's appearance.
- Do not claim success or end the instance until the environment indicates it is over.
